title: Savoy Will Observe Its 70th Anniversary Late In October
text:
MONDAY, JANUARY 19, 1942

Savoy Will Observe Its 70th Anniversary Late In October

Col. Savoy Gave Railroad Forty Acres For Town

Charter Granted For Town In 1873, One Of Oldest In This Area

By JAMES ELIZABETH LARGE

SAVOY, Jan. 19.—In 1872 Col. Savoy made a contract with the Transcontinental Railway now known as the T. & P. for 40 acres of land on which to build a town if they would build a railroad through the town on land donated. To this they agreed and a deed was given Bonham Oct. 29, 1872. Twenty acres on each side of the track. On Aug. 8, 1873, the charter for the town was granted. Records show that some of the lots sold for as much as $80.

The depot was erected where the present one now stands. Savoy's first business house was erected on Front street and Main street on the south side of the railroad. Hodgson and Beard owned and operated a general merchandise store. The first saloon to be put up was on Front but on the east side of Main street, R. T. Tear opened a saloon. These were Savoy's first merchants.

Until now the only means of obtaining supplies was to haul from Bonham and Denison and sometimes more distant points, this being done with a horse and team, taking several days or weeks to make the round trip. By the time there has now grown to a thriving little village, the census is in a couple of months.

The prosperity continued until May 28, 1880, when the terrible cyclone hit the town. Savoy being the exact date and time by the people was by Johnnie Weir.

'Twas in the spring of '80

Had Flour Mill

In the fall of 1900 there was a flour mill here, located north of the old school building. In 1902 a new elevator was built, known as the Womack Milling Co. It was a place of milling for several years before it was torn down. Until recent years there has been a cotton gin here at one time and at night in the fall. They now have a modern gin up and have not been replaced.

It was replaced by a brick structure. Savoy, unlike so many places its size, still has an Agency and telegraph office, is still served by the Texas & Pacific Railway. Although there are only two passenger trains daily, there were formerly six.

There are six grocery stores, four filling stations, one drug store, two dry goods shops, two blacksmith shops, two produce houses, one cafe, one meat market, one dress and hat shop and some dry goods store.

Had Telephone System

The first telephone switchboard was owned by the late Tom Frank, with Miss Etta King, now Mrs. Etta McMahon, as operator. Mr. Frank sold the board and it was run by Joe Savoy Star office, with Miss Almeda running the board for several years. With the help of her sister, Miss Almeda and Miss Anna. After Miss Almeda married and Miss Anna took a position away from Savoy, Miss Anna Owens, operator. After several years Miss Owens accepted a position in Sherman, Miss Velma Boothe, who is now Mrs. Velma Boothe Woodard[?] was made manager, and still holds the position. The system is owned by the Southwestern Bell Telephone Co.

First Public Water Well

The first public water well was drilled in H. H. Beard's yard in the fall of 1913, and was operated by J. L. Riley. When he sold it and moved to Nevada, there were no other available times, and did not wait for the ones who went to the expense for the larger part of the school bell[?] that went through the fire and is using it for a door stop.

Joe Noah Was Carrier

Joe Noah, it is said, was the first rural mail carrier at Savoy. E. A. Spaddow, now of Dallas; Will McMcSpaddow, carried on the route out of town, and the late R. C. Frank McMaddow[?]. Not long after, until the consolidation of the routes, Jim McMaddow's route was the one to go. Mr. McMaddow's record shows there were four teachers then. The first appointment of Miller of Denison exchanged routes with his death. Miller and Owens both [?], then the routes were combined. Owens going to Mahurin and he replaced Miller. Dodson was sent to Bonham, replaced it, this time one story. The school here is provided with modern equipment. There is a modern rock gym on the west, where the F. F. A. class meets, and the bot[?] 13 tennis room is located. There are 13 telephone directors, two recreation directors, six employed in the lunch room. The Randolph Grove school has been consolidated with the Savoy school, the New Warren school, transferred to the Mahurin was also transferred.

90-Year-Old Citizen

One of Fannie County's oldest citizens resides in Savoy. He is A. Deatherage. He celebrated his ninety-fourth birthday March 22. He was born in Tennessee, came to Texas at the age of 5 with his parents in 1853, has lived within a radius of five miles of Savoy the rest of his life. He was married to Miss Sally Ray Aug. 19, 1875. She died about three years ago. They have eight living children and 15 living grandchildren, several great-grandchildren.

The Savoy Methodist Church was organized in 1873 by the Rev. Graves of Sherman. The building was erected the same year. The lot was given by Col. Savoy and the first load of lumber was hauled from Bells by the late T. W. McSpadden. Most of the members moved away. All denominations except the Seventh Day Adventists used the building for worship.

Baptist Church Founded

The first Baptist Church of the Savoy community was across from Jerdon, located east of town. Many of the older members of the present church united with it in their early childhood. Some time after the original building burned, the church was organized. The Little Church moved back into town and moved to Ector to be rebuilt and before it was completed it was moved back to Savoy. A new church was built. Most of the members moved their membership to the Savoy church. The reorganization of the present church organization took place. Several older members who were interviewed, some time near 1880.

The exact date of the organization of the first Church of Christ in Savoy is not known to any of the older members, but the first organization was before Savoy was a town. It was organized in the Roberts school house south of Savoy. The first officers were Jeff Clevenger, O. H. Clevenger, William Francis and J. J. Jenkins, Sr. At that time there were about 40 members and five of the Jenkins children were members. Also, Mrs. Ada L. Travis of Hondo, Texas and Joseph Savoy of Mission, Texas. Both still living at the time. Mrs. Ada L. Travis was a Spanish war veteran and [rest of column cut off]

Ed McMahon, 79, Dies
